roles.heroLead: A 1926 Ballard craftsman and a brand-new Beacon Hill townhome fail the same way: water gets past grout that was never waterproof to begin with. The membrane behind the tile is the actual product — so we build that assembly first, flood it for 24 hours, keep photographic proof, and only then set tile. Old-house surprises included; drama not.

roles.costH2: How much does tile installation cost in Seattle, WA?
roles.costP1: Installed tile in Seattle runs $14–$26 per square foot when tile, setting materials, substrate prep and labor are totaled honestly; the labor component alone begins at $11/sq ft. A tub-shower surround usually bills $3,200–$6,800, and a full bath — floor, shower, niche — commonly closes between $6,500 and $14,000.
roles.costP2: City-house truth: format beats price. A cheap penny-round sheet can cost more to install than a spendy large-format plank, because the labor follows the cut count and the linear feet of grout joints — numbers the price sticker never mentions.
roles.costNote: Seattle installed ranges as of August 2026, tile + materials + labor. Old-house framing can shift them either way, which is exactly what the free written estimate is for.
roles.layersLead: Seven layers stand between your framing and the grout line. In every failed Seattle shower we open — craftsman, mid-century or brand-new — one layer got skipped, and it is almost always the membrane, traded once for a few hundred dollars and paid back at demolition prices.
roles.whyP1: In a hundred-year-old house the leak has more places to hide: it travels a joist bay, skips a room, and appears as a warped fir floor two rooms over or a bubble in the plaster below. However far it wanders, the destination is the same invoice — framing, subfloor, drywall, and the tile all over again.
roles.whyP2: Waterproofing is a tenth of what the shower costs. Against what Seattle framing repairs bill at, it is the best-priced insurance in the building.
roles.scopeIntro: Entry prices; the tile's shape, what we find under the old floor and the layout's fussiness move them. The dependable number is the written one, produced free at your house.
roles.cardShower: Waterproofed from the framing out: pre-sloped pan, bonded membrane, documented overnight flood test — then the visible part with niche and curb or curbless entry. You pay for the layer you never see again.
roles.cardFloors: Craftsman baths, condo kitchens, basement suites, entries. Floors get flattened first — non-negotiable in older houses — and an uncoupling membrane wherever the structure or a heat mat calls for it.
roles.cardBacksplash: Subway to zellige to slab-look. Cuts land clean around outlets, edges get real trim, and the grout is matched to your counters instead of whatever the box suggested.
roles.cardHeated: Electric mats over uncoupling membrane, resistance-verified before and after tile, on a dedicated circuit. In an old Seattle house it is the difference between a bathroom and a warm one.
roles.cardRepair: Cracks, failing grout, shower corners opening up. We diagnose whether it is a surface repair or a substrate problem wearing a disguise — and quote only for the true one.
roles.cardDemo: Original tile, mud beds, backer — out to clean framing with sheeting and negative air protecting the rest of the house, then hauled away. Century-old debris weighs plenty; that is our problem.

roles.faqQ1: How much does tile installation cost in Seattle, WA?
roles.faqA1: Seattle tile installation totals roughly $14 to $26 per square foot installed — tile, setting materials, prep and labor combined — and labor on its own opens at $11 per square foot. Shower surrounds price around $3,200 to $6,800; complete bathrooms with floor, shower and niche run $6,500 to $14,000 in most cases. The tile's format moves the bill more than its unit price: mosaics and very large planks both take substantially more labor than 12×12 field tile.
roles.faqQ2: How much does it cost to tile a shower in Seattle?
roles.faqA2: Plan on $3,200 to $6,800 for a standard Seattle alcove shower, inclusive of demolition, bonded waterproofing, pre-sloped base, tile setting, a niche and grout. Steam showers, benches, curbless entries and full-height stone push past that range. Roughly a tenth of the budget is the waterproofing — the tenth that prevents the tens-of-thousands failure.
roles.faqQ3: Do you waterproof showers before tiling?
roles.faqA3: Always — a bonded system per TCNA / ANSI A118.10, not cement board with hope on top. That means the pre-sloped base, a sheet or liquid membrane up the walls, sealed corners, seams and pipe penetrations, then a plugged drain and 24 hours under standing water, photographed, before the first tile touches thinset. Grout is porous; the membrane is the waterproofing.
roles.faqQ4: How long does a bathroom tile job take?
roles.faqA4: A Seattle bathroom typically needs four to six working days — demolition and dust walls, then substrate plus membrane with the flood test sitting overnight, then one to two days of setting once the test passes, and finally grout, silicone and trim. The shower cures another 24 hours before first use. In craftsman homes, add a contingency day for what the old floor hides.
roles.faqQ5: Porcelain or ceramic tile — which is better?
roles.faqA5: Porcelain wherever water or traffic lives: it absorbs less than 0.5% water, resists chips, and carries heavy use without complaint. Ceramic is the sensible wall-and-backsplash material at a friendlier price. Our Seattle rule of thumb — porcelain underfoot and in showers, ceramic and glass up on the walls where they belong.
roles.faqQ6: Can you install a heated tile floor?
roles.faqA6: Yes, and in drafty older Seattle houses it earns its keep fast: an electric radiant mat adds about $11 to $16 per square foot installed with the thermostat. It lays over an uncoupling membrane, gets resistance-tested both before and after setting, and runs on its own circuit. The economics only work while the floor is already open, so decide during the remodel, not after.
roles.faqQ7: Do I need to remove the old tile first?
roles.faqA7: Almost always — and in older Seattle homes especially, where original mud-set floors conceal the subfloor's condition. Removal with haul-away is about $3.50 per square foot and buys the only honest inspection you will get, plus correct finished heights at doorways. Tiling over tile is reserved for genuinely flat, tightly bonded floors, and even then it hides what demolition would reveal.
roles.faqQ8: How much does a kitchen backsplash cost in Seattle?
roles.faqA8: For the common 30-square-foot run, Seattle backsplashes come in at $1,100 to $2,200 installed — outlet cuts, edge trim and matched grout included. Mosaic sheets, herringbone lays, picture-frame details behind ranges and slab-look full-height porcelain land at the top of that band on cutting and layout time alone.
roles.faqQ9: Can you fix cracked tile or regrout instead of replacing?
roles.faqA9: Regularly — repair and regrout starts around $8 per square foot and suits stained or failing grout, isolated impact cracks, and shower corners due for silicone. The exception: tile sounding hollow, popping loose in a spreading area, or walls with flex underneath. That is the substrate talking, a patch merely delays it, and we will identify which conversation you are in before any quote.
roles.faqQ10: Which Seattle neighborhoods do you tile?
roles.faqA10: Across the city: Ballard, Wallingford, Fremont, Green Lake, Phinney Ridge, Greenwood, Queen Anne, Magnolia, Capitol Hill, Ravenna, Maple Leaf, Wedgwood, Beacon Hill, Columbia City, Mount Baker and West Seattle among them — plus Shoreline, Bellevue, Mercer Island, Renton and the Eastside when the job calls.
roles.faqQ11: What warranty comes with tile installation?
roles.faqA11: A 2-year workmanship warranty backs every OC Flooring tile job — longer than our carpet coverage on purpose, since tile defects reveal themselves in the second year rather than the first fortnight. Complete manufacturer waterproofing assemblies add the system warranty from the maker, and our photos of the membrane and flood test keep the record straight for any future sale.
